column2: The notes explain the main numbers. Always read these:
Sales of each product and big customers; the cost of making things (materials, wages, energy); side income and costs.
Deals with related companies; money owed by customers and how old it is; the warehouse; loans (interest, due date, dollar or rial).
Unfinished projects; debts and commitments that might arise; events after the end of the year.
A financial statement is like a repair shop’s invoice: you see the total at the bottom, but you have to read the parts and labour on the back.
The 10 notes you always read
Signs of a healthy company: most of its profit comes from its main work, profit per unit is steady or improving, and real cash comes in at the same size as profit.
Its reports are clear and on time, it has few corrections, and the auditor found no important problems.
Unhealthy signs: big gains from selling land or shares, debts owed to and by the company that keep growing, and unclear deals with related companies.
Back-to-back capital increases to “fix the financial structure” and changing auditors often are also warning bells.
A trader whose income comes from selling goods is healthy; one who sells a piece of the shop every year to look profitable isn’t.
Healthy and unhealthy companies
First read the top of the page: what report it is and how many months it covers. The numbers add up from the start of the financial year, not just the last three months.
Not every company’s financial year ends in Esfand; check the date carefully.
The unit is “million rials”. 4,814,954 million rials is about 481 billion tomans. Earnings per share (EPS) are always in rials.
If “unregistered capital” is above zero, a capital increase is on the way.
Like reading an electricity bill: first see how many months it covers and what the unit is, then judge the number.
Each number is compared with the same period last year, not the previous quarter. Last three months = 9 months minus 6 months.
A number in brackets means negative, for example a cost.
The percentage change is written from profit’s point of view: a cost that fell has a positive number because it helps profit.
“--” means it went from loss to profit or the other way round, and “restated” means last year’s numbers were corrected.
If this year’s gas bill is 20% lower than last year’s, that’s good news for your pocket; the report also shows a lower cost as positive.
This table is from a real Codal report (the company’s name isn’t shown). This lesson’s exercises use this table.
Sales are only 3% higher, but the cost of making things is 41% lower; that’s why operating profit more than doubled.
Net earnings per share went from 243 to 472 rials, while capital also went up.
Like a restaurant whose customers are about the same but which bought meat much cheaper; its profit doubled with flat sales. The key question: will the cheap buying repeat?
“Other expenses” above operating profit is different from “other income” lower down the page.
Prior years’ tax means old tax that came in higher than expected; if it repeats every year, the company is under-counting tax.
Set aside profit from closed-down parts of the business when looking at lasting profit.
The nominal value of each share is 1,000 rials; so the number of shares = capital in rials ÷ 1,000, and earnings per share = net profit ÷ number of shares.
If a company has 1,000 million rials of profit and 500 million shares, earnings per share are 2 rials.
Funds don’t have sales or production costs; their reports are net assets, profit and loss, and asset movements.
A fund’s assets also grow when new money comes in; so that isn’t a measure of how good it is. The measure is the value of each unit (NAV).
The manager’s, auditor’s and other fees are a real cost to you.
Three questions: did each unit’s value grow more than the index? What percentage of assets are the fees? What shares has it put money into?
A restaurant with more customers doesn’t necessarily have better food; a busy fund also just means more money came in, not that its return is better.
Read each report in 10 minutes like this:
Look at the header. Compare sales growth with inflation. Work out the profit per unit of sales (margin) for this year and last.
Separate side income and costs. Look at the tax rate. Check earnings per share against capital.
Read the note on correcting last year’s numbers and write down three questions; don’t draw a conclusion until you’ve found their answers.
Like a 10-minute check of a used car: papers, mileage, oil, tyres, paint; always in the same order so nothing is missed.
